title: Permutations of a String
excerpt: Two standard ways to generate permutations, why they need different duplicate tests, and why only the bottom row of the tree counts as an answer this time.

content.text: Printing every permutation of a string is the standard second backtracking exercise, and it introduces something subsets did not have: a real distinction between a partial state and an answer.

In the subsets tree, every node was an answer. Here only the leaves are. A half-built permutation is not a permutation of anything, so the recording step moves to the bottom of the tree and the internal nodes become pure scaffolding.
Both are common enough that you should recognise either on sight.

content.text: Switch between the two methods below on the same input. The answers match; the order they arrive in does not, and neither does what the array looks like part way down.

In used-array mode, watch the free-characters panel shrink as you descend and refill as you back out. That panel is the boolean array, and it is the entire difference between this and an unconstrained loop.

Then switch to swap mode and watch the array itself change. The swap-back frame after each branch is the un-choose step. Remove it and the array drifts, so the next branch permutes something that was never the input.

Give the string AAB to the naive version and it emits six results, of which only three are different. The two As are distinguishable by index and by nothing else, so the algorithm faithfully produces each ordering twice.
Switch the input to AAB above and turn duplicate skipping on. The rejected branches show up in coral: those are the subtrees that would have rebuilt work already done.
The fix depends on which method you are using, and this is the part that catches people who have memorised one of them.

rows: skip if i > 0 and s[i] === s[i-1] and not used[i-1]
Equal characters sit next to each other. Only let the leftmost unused one go first, so a fixed representative is chosen each time.
keep a set of values already placed at this depth; skip repeats
Swapping destroys sortedness, so the neighbour test is meaningless. The set is per level, not global.

content.text: The
!used[i-1]

half of the first test is the subtle bit. Without it you also block the legitimate case where the previous equal character is already placed higher up the current path, and you lose real answers rather than duplicates.

variants.code:
# Used-array version. Sort first if you want duplicate skipping
# or lexicographic output.
def permutations(s, dedupe=False):
    chars = sorted(s) if dedupe else list(s)
    used = [False] * len(chars)
    out = []
    current = []

    def backtrack():
        if len(current) == len(chars):
            out.append("".join(current))
            return

        for i in range(len(chars)):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            # Only the leftmost unused copy of a repeated character may go first.
            if dedupe and i > 0 and chars[i] == chars[i - 1] and not used[i - 1]:
                continue

            used[i] = True
            current.append(chars[i])    # choose
            backtrack()                 # explore
            current.pop()               # un-choose
            used[i] = False

    backtrack()
    return out


# Swap version. No extra array, but the output is not sorted.
def permutations_by_swap(s):
    chars = list(s)
    out = []

    def backtrack(k):
        if k == len(chars):
            out.append("".join(chars))
            return
        seen = set()
        for i in range(k, len(chars)):
            if chars[i] in seen:        # duplicate test, per level
                continue
            seen.add(chars[i])

            chars[k], chars[i] = chars[i], chars[k]   # choose
            backtrack(k + 1)                          # explore
            chars[k], chars[i] = chars[i], chars[k]   # un-choose

    backtrack(0)
    return out

content.text: There are n! permutations and each one takes O(n) to write out, so no algorithm can beat O(n · n!) if it has to produce all of them. Both versions here hit that bound. The output is the bottleneck, not the search.

This is worth internalising before optimising anything: 10 characters is 3.6 million permutations, 13 is over six billion. If a problem asks for all permutations of anything longer than about ten items, the problem is usually not really asking for that.

questions.prompt: Why can't the swap method use the s[i] === s[i-1] duplicate test?

options.label: Swapping destroys the sorted order the test depends on
The swap method cannot produce duplicates at all
It can, but it is slower

questions.prompt: In the permutations tree, which nodes are answers?

options.label: Only the leaves, since a partial permutation is not a permutation

questions.prompt: What is the unavoidable time complexity of listing every permutation of n distinct characters?

options.label: O(n · n!), because there are n! outputs each of length n

content.text: The used-array version, drawn out:
Compare it against the subsets chart. The loop runs over all n characters instead of a suffix, because any unused character may come next, and there is an extra
used[i] ?
decision whose "yes" branch skips the character entirely. The choose step now sets two things rather than one, and the un-choose step has to undo both.
The stopping test also moved: it is
current.length == n
at the top rather than a record-on-entry, which is the structural expression of "only the leaves are answers here".
